explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul, the apostle writing this letter, says, “…I received it by revelation from Jesus Christ.” He says he didn't get it from any man, and he wasn't taught it either. He also says the gospel he preached was not devised by man. No middleman. Not one.

explanations.answer: From the teachers of the Law
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but Paul shuts that door himself. He says, “I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it…” Teachers are people, so they're out. Paul says he received it “…by revelation from Jesus Christ.” I once got a recipe from a takeout menu in a junk drawer, and even THAT had a source.

explanations.answer: From the elders of the churches
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd guess that, friend. But Paul says he did not receive the gospel from any man, nor was he taught it. Elders are men, so that's not his answer. He says, “…I received it by revelation from Jesus Christ.” He also says the gospel he preached was not devised by man.

explanations.answer: Persecuted it and tried to destroy it
explanations.explanation: Yes, and Paul doesn't hide it. He says, “…how severely I persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it.” That's a heavy thing to admit about yourself. I think it took guts to put it in a letter. He tells it straight, and he tells it first.

explanations.answer: Joined it and taught its people
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Paul says about his old life, friend. Back then he persecuted the church. He says he “…tried to destroy it.” Joining and teaching comes later in his story. This part is the hard part, and I think Paul says it plainly on purpose.

explanations.answer: Left it alone and moved away
explanations.explanation: If only it were that quiet, friend. Paul didn't leave the church alone. He says he “…severely” persecuted it and tried to destroy it. That's a heavy line, and he doesn't soften it. Moving away isn't anywhere in his account.

Zealous is the word, baker. Paul says he was “…extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers.” That's all-in, no half measures. Me, I'm zealous about exactly one thing, and it's stamping cookies before the oven goes cold.

Not even close, friend. Paul wasn't unsure about anything back then. He says he was “…extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers.” Zealous means he cared a LOT and pushed hard. Unsure would be me standing at the oven asking if it's on.

Careless is more my speed with oven mitts, friend. Paul was the opposite. He says he was “…extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers.” Zealous means he threw his whole self into it. Nothing careless about that.

Paul says the exact reverse, friend. He writes, “I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries…” That means he was ahead of many people his own age, not trailing behind. He wasn't coasting back there. He was out front.

That's right, baker. Paul says, “I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries…” His contemporaries are the people his own age. So he was ahead of many of them, not falling behind. Paul didn't need a trophy for that. He just told the Galatians how it was.

Gentiles it is, baker. Paul says God was pleased to reveal His Son in him “…so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles…” Gentiles are people who aren't Jewish. And that's who Paul would preach to. Look at that, the man who started out against the church ends up carrying the news.

Priests don't show up in this verse, friend. Paul says God revealed His Son in him “…so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles…” Gentiles are people who aren't Jewish. That's the group Paul names, so that's the group the verse is about.

I get the guess, friend, but the verse names a different group. Paul says the purpose was “…so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles…” Gentiles are people who aren't Jewish. The Pharisees aren't mentioned anywhere in this passage.

Paul says no, friend. He writes, “…I did not rush to consult with flesh and blood…” Flesh and blood means people. He didn't go running to ask anybody about it. Me, I'd have been on the phone before the glow even faded.

That's right, baker. Paul says, “…I did not rush to consult with flesh and blood…” He didn't go sprinting around asking people what to think. Kevin Hart would have told the whole town in ten minutes. Paul took another road, and we'll see which one next.

explanations.answer: Into Arabia and later back to Damascus
explanations.explanation: Arabia and then back to Damascus, baker. Paul says he did not go up to Jerusalem to the apostles who came before him. Instead he says, “…I went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus.” Notice the word returned. He had been in Damascus before he went.

explanations.answer: Into Egypt and later back to Joppa
explanations.explanation: Those are real places, friend, but they're not Paul's. He says, “…I went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus.” Egypt and Joppa don't appear in this passage. I'd need a map AND a timer to keep up with this man.

explanations.answer: Into Macedonia and later back to Antioch
explanations.explanation: Good travel plan, friend, but it's not what Paul wrote. He says, “…I went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus.” Macedonia and Antioch don't come up in these verses. Paul names his stops, and these aren't on the list.

Cephas is right, baker. That's the name Jesus gave Simon, which means Peter (John 1:42). Paul says he went up to confer with him and stayed fifteen days. Fifteen days is a good long visit. I think that's plenty of time to talk.

Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus (Acts 4:36), isn't named in this passage, friend. Paul says he went up to Jerusalem “…to confer with Cephas…” Cephas is the name Jesus gave Simon, which means Peter (John 1:42). Paul stayed with him fifteen days.

Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit (Acts 6:5), doesn't appear in these verses, friend. Paul says he went up “…to confer with Cephas…” That's Peter, whom Jesus called Cephas (John 1:42). And Paul stayed with him fifteen days.

That's right, baker. Paul says, “But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord's brother.” So Cephas and James are the two he mentions. It's a short guest list. I've had longer ones for a Tuesday batch.

Actually, friend, it's true. Paul says, “But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord's brother.” So besides Cephas, James is the only one he names. That's the whole list for that trip.

explanations.answer: The regions of Syria and Cilicia
explanations.explanation: Syria and Cilicia, baker. Paul says, “Later I went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia.” He keeps moving, one region after another. A man who stays in one oven all his life has no idea what's out there. I would know, I spent years in a drawer.

explanations.answer: The regions of Pontus and Bithynia
explanations.explanation: Those are real places, friend, but they aren't in Paul's list. He says, “Later I went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia.” Pontus and Bithynia don't appear in this passage. Paul names his stops, so we stick to his.

explanations.answer: The regions of Galatia and Phrygia
explanations.explanation: Galatia is where this letter is headed, friend (Galatians 1:2). But that's not where Paul says he went next. He says, “Later I went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia.” Phrygia doesn't come up in these verses.

Paul says it the other way, friend. He writes, “I was personally unknown, however, to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.” So they didn't know his face. They only knew of him. Famous on paper and a stranger in person, that's a strange spot to be.

That's right, baker. Paul says, “I was personally unknown, however, to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.” They didn't know him in person. Whatever they knew came from what they heard. Next verse tells us what that was.

Preaching, baker. The churches hear, “The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” Read that slow. The same man, the same faith, but now he's preaching it instead of fighting it. That's quite a turn.

Doubting isn't in the verse, friend. The churches hear, “The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” Paul isn't wavering about the faith. He's preaching it. That's the news that traveled.

Avoiding would be a small change, friend. But the report says he “…is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” He isn't dodging it. He's out preaching it. That's the part that got people talking.

explanations.answer: They glorify God because of Paul
explanations.explanation: They did, baker. Paul says, “And they glorified God because of me.” They heard the news and gave God the glory. Paul doesn't say they gave him the credit. I think he wanted it that way.

explanations.answer: They send men to question Paul
explanations.explanation: That's not how the verse ends, friend. Paul writes, “And they glorified God because of me.” Nothing here about sending anyone to question him. These churches heard the story and turned to God.
Hard to blame anyone for guessing that, friend, given Paul's past. But he says, “And they glorified God because of me.” No warnings are mentioned. The churches heard the news and glorified God.
